title: map, filter, find, and reduce
runtime: Modern evergreen browser or Node.js with ES modules. Run fragments in browser DevTools or a small .js file unless the example says otherwise.

objectives.text: Use map when every input becomes an output.
Use filter to keep matching items.
Use find when only the first match is needed.
Use reduce when many values become one result.

learningFlow: Explain the result in your own words
Apply the idea in a different problem
Review after two and seven days

diagnostic.question: Can you explain the main purpose of map, filter, find, and reduce before reading?
diagnostic.answer: A complete answer should name the problem it solves, the values or control flow involved, and one mistake to avoid.

sections.title: map transforms
sections.body: map calls a function for each array item and returns a new array of the same length. The callback result becomes the corresponding output item. Use it for transforming data or creating JSX lists, and always return the intended value from a block-bodied callback.

sections.title: filter selects
sections.body: filter keeps each original item whose callback returns truthy. It returns a new array and may return zero, some, or all items. It does not transform kept items; chain map separately when both selection and transformation are required.

sections.title: find returns one item
sections.body: find stops at the first matching item and returns that item, or undefined if none matches. findIndex returns the index instead. Handle the missing case before reading properties from the result.

sections.title: reduce accumulates
sections.body: reduce carries an accumulator through the array. Give an explicit initial value so empty arrays and result types are predictable. It works for totals, grouped objects, and other summaries, but a loop can be clearer when the accumulator becomes complicated.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: map, filter, find, and reduce is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain map, filter, find, and reduce to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Use map when every input becomes an output. Use filter to keep matching items. Use find when only the first match is needed. Use reduce when many values become one result.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using map, filter, find, and reduce behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can map, filter, find, and reduce affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using map, filter, find, and reduce produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
